text: The same test explains a sentence that has surprised readers who expect tragedy to deal in greatness. "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). Johnson meant this as praise. The heroes of other dramatists speak a language that no living person ever used, swollen by the poet's wish to astonish; their passions are pitched above the occasion, and their words climb after the passion until the audience can admire but can no longer believe. Shakespeare's persons speak as the reader himself would have spoken had he stood where they stand, with the same fears and the same plain anger. This holds even where the action leaves the ordinary world. A play may bring a ghost upon the stage or set witches on a heath, and the plot may turn on events that nobody has ever witnessed; yet the men and women who meet these wonders answer them in the speech of common life. Johnson counted this among the surest marks of the poet's power. The story may grow strange, but the dialogue stays level with experience, and the man who confronts a spirit replies to it as a merchant or a soldier of Johnson's London would have replied.
